text: Many harness fit badly because a large part of the trade refuses to measure the horse; some straps can be adjusted with buckles, but the principal ones cannot and must be the right length from the start.
The hame tug is prominent among the straps whose length cannot be adjusted afterwards, whether for a short tug or a long tug harness.
On a long tug harness the hame tug must be of such length that, with the collar well down on the shoulder, the market tug follows a line parallel with the center of the pad side.

If the market tug does not lie parallel with the center of the pad side, an unnecessary strain is thrown on the swivel or loop in the end of the pad top, and the pad is likely to be drawn out of shape.

If a short tug is long enough for the trace buckle to touch the pad trace bearer on a double harness, or the buckle on the back-band of a single harness, those straps or the hame tug itself will be injured.
The length of the horse from the collar to the girth is an important measurement because it governs the hame tug.

On a breast collar harness, if the neck strap tugs are set too far back the collar sags in front and interferes with the horse's movement, or the neck strap must be shortened so much that it is strained when the trace is straightened.
Large manufacturers who cannot measure every horse use a set of lengths for each class of harness, based on the size of horse it is meant for.
A coach harness is cut for horses sixteen hands high or over.
A double road harness is cut for horses fifteen or fifteen and a half hands high.
A light phaeton harness is cut for horses fourteen or fourteen and a half hands high.
A light track harness is cut to fit a horse fifteen or fifteen and a half hands high.
A coupe harness is cut for horses sixteen to sixteen and a half hands high.
Regular buggy harness for common use is cut with traces and other lengthwise straps to fit horses fifteen hands high, but the girths are cut for heavier animals.

One rule starts from the lengths suited to a fifteen-hand horse and, for every hand of increase or decrease in the horse's size, adds or subtracts four inches on girths, one and one half inches on breast and breeching bodies, and three inches on hip and neck straps.

To measure for a bridle cheek piece, take the length from the corner of the mouth to one inch below the root of the ear, add enough for the lap that secures the buckle, and add two thirds of the original length.
A cheek piece cut by the two-thirds rule is long enough for the loose end to enter the cheek loop about one half its length.

To measure for a crown piece, measure from the root of the ear on one side, over the head, to the root of the ear on the other side, and add five or six inches to each end for the cheek and throat latch billets.
To measure for a throat latch, measure from a point two inches below the root of the ear, around the throat, to the corresponding point on the other side.
To measure the neck strap for a breast collar, pass the measure over the neck just forward of the highest point of the withers and carry the ends forward three inches.

To find the length of a breast collar, measure from a point four inches above the elbow on one side, around the breast just below where the throat enters the breast, to the same point on the other side.
For a harness with a long tug and market tug, measure from the end of the hame draft eye to the center of the girth, and deduct the length of the buckle back of the center of the loop.
When measuring for the hame tug, the collar must sit well back in its place, because a tug that is too long or too short keeps the market tug out of its proper position.
To measure for the breeching, draw the line around the buttock from a point just above the stifle to the same point on the opposite side, and allow one inch for slack.
To measure for hip straps, measure from a point ten inches forward of the crupper down to the point occupied by the body of the breeching, and deduct three inches for the breeching tugs.
A set of lengths suited to horses in one locality may be partly unsuited to those of another because the horses differ in build, so furnished lengths should be tested before being adopted in full.
